doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

title: Coltrane, Eric Dolphy and the 245 Carlton Avenue house in Brooklyn
summary: Ridley lived in Slide Hampton's Brooklyn brownstone with Hubbard and others, and got to know John Coltrane there; he also mentions Papa Jo Jones and Coleman Hawkins.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Coltrane. John Coltrane was one of the most humble people that you ever wanted to — and one of the most focused people. Eric Dolphy. Eric Dolphy, we lived, a bunch of us lived in the same house. See how I got to know Coltrane personally, I had met him in the fifties but I had really got to know him because I lived at this house. When you see on Eric Dolphy’s record “245” — 245 was the address of a brownstone that Slide Hampton owned in Brooklyn. 245 Carleton Avenue. And Charles Greenlee was married to Coltrane’s cousin Mary.

Yes. So he lived in the house, and she’s like my sister you know. And Billy Fraser, Slide Hampton, all of us, Freddie Hubbard, we all lived in that house. And there was so much music and Yusef Lateef and all kinds of people would come through the house. And Coltrane and I used to go out to Coltrane’s house and hang out with him. I knew him man, I knew this guy. And he was so beautiful and so focused. Sonny Rollins man, Wynton Kelly man, all these guys man, Philly Jo Jones took me on like a little brother, taught me so much. Papa Jo Jones. And Coleman Hawkins. When I worked with Coleman Hawkins I used to just sit up for hours with him just asking him. Because I wanted to know more of the — I had an acquaintancship with Leonard Feather and we would talk and I had a great deal of respect for Leonard Feather and his role.
